claim_as_stated: Vanguard agreed to acquire Altruist on 2026-08-26, and ~6 weeks later Altruist launched DAFs sponsored by Endaoment
exact_values_found: Definitive agreement announced 2026-08-26; terms undisclosed (WSJ ~$4bn unconfirmed); close expected later in 2026 subject to approvals; Altruist to run standalone. WealthManagement.com article datePublished 2026-10-06T04:01Z: DAF accounts 'sponsored by Endaoment, a 501(c)(3) public charity that is the legal owner of DAF assets and the customer of record'; no account/balance/grant minimums; fees start at 50 bps vs 60-65 bps 'typical'. Interval = 41 days (~6 weeks).
discrepancies: None material. Deal was signed, not closed; 'acquire' should stay 'agreed to acquire'.
interpretation_challenge: Timing does not show Vanguard caused or approved the Endaoment choice; the DAF product was likely in build before the deal. Endaoment approval of grants/investments retained ('subject to Endaoment's approval'). 50 bps is Altruist's stated starting fee, not total cost.

entity: Bain Capital / Ren / Envestnet; GTCR / Foundation Source / AssetMark
claim_as_stated: Bain Capital holds a majority of Ren and also owns Envestnet; Envestnet chose Foundation Source for DAFs. GTCR owns both Foundation Source and AssetMark; AssetMark uses TIFIN Give.
exact_values_found: Great Hill release (2025-10-28): 'Bain Capital Tech Opportunities, which acquired a majority stake in Ren in 2023, will remain a significant shareholder'. Bain Capital affiliates closed Envestnet take-private 2024-11-25 ($63.15/sh, ~$4.5bn; Reverence, Norwest, BlackRock, Fidelity, Franklin, SSGA minority). Foundation Source-Envestnet integration (Sept 2025) covers private foundations, DAFs and planned giving plus admin/compliance/tax services; firms 'separate and unaffiliated'. GTCR acquired Foundation Source (announced 2023-09-13) and AssetMark (~$2.7bn, closed 2024-09). AssetMark DAF: TIFIN WealthTech LLC platform with GiveClear Foundation as 501(c)(3) sponsor (June 2024).
discrepancies: Present-tense 'holds a majority' is not supported after the Oct 2025 Great Hill round: the release says Bain 'acquired a majority stake ... in 2023' and 'will remain a significant shareholder'; current majority holder undisclosed. Ren and Envestnet sit in different Bain funds (Tech Opportunities vs Bain Capital PE-led consortium). 'Chose Foundation Source for DAFs' overstates exclusivity: Envestnet also lists GiftingNetwork, and the FS integration is broader than DAFs. AssetMark's sponsor is GiveClear, not TIFIN.
interpretation_challenge: Common ownership does not imply coordinated product choice; portfolio companies of the same PE sponsor routinely pick rival vendors. The 'Ren's rival' framing is the repo's inference.

claim_as_stated: Shift4 wrote down The Giving Block earnout by $47.1M within a year against a $246M maximum (SEC filings)
exact_values_found: FY2022 10-K: 'Shift4 Payments, Inc. recognized fair value adjustments to the contingent liability for The Giving Block of $(47.1) million for the year ended December 31, 2022'; CAM: earnout 'not to exceed $246.0 million'; contingent consideration at 2022-02-28 $57.8m (of $111.1m total consideration; cash $16.8m + shares $36.4m + RSUs $0.1m = $53.3m non-contingent; $106.9m net of $4.2m cash acquired). Earnout liability $59.2m at 2022-03-31, $10.9m at 2022-12-31 (parent-level), $2.9m at 2023-03-31 (cash portion) after a further $(0.5)m Q1-2023 adjustment.
discrepancies: 'Wrote down' describes a reduction of a liability (a gain in 'Revaluation of contingent liabilities'), not an asset impairment. Repo's '$54m upfront' is approximate ($53.3m gross non-contingent). Repo cites Payments Dive and Financial_Report.xlsx rather than the 10-K text.
interpretation_challenge: A falling earnout liability means TGB revenue in the Mar-2022 to Feb-2023 window came in far below the forecast that priced it (crypto downturn); it is evidence about TGB revenue, not about DAF economics. 'Within a year' = ~10 months (2022-02-28 to 2022-12-31).

claim_as_stated: Fidelity Charitable's 2026 Giving Report states 67% of grants are paid by EFT; Fidelity's pages say it 'does not currently require EFT enrollment'
exact_values_found: Report: 'Today, 67% of our grants are distributed via EFT, meaning that more than 2 million grants have reached nonprofits faster...'; '98% of grant recommendations were initiated digitally' in 2025; 3 million grants in 2025. FAQ: 'While we do not currently require EFT enrollment for nonprofit organizations'; 'As Fidelity Charitable moves towards a digital-first policy we are transitioning grant payments to EFT'; never-enrolled nonprofits 'receive grants through checks'.
discrepancies: Report says 'distributed via EFT', not 'paid'; immaterial. Report contains no EFT-only date. Repo red-team note says '(about 1m checks in 2025)' - not in the report; 33% of ~3m grants is an inference.
contradictory_evidence: Chariot (Mar 2026) reported a July 2026 move to electronic-only; not reflected on Fidelity's live FAQ.
interpretation_challenge: '67% of our grants' is ambiguous between a 2025 share and a cumulative share ('more than 2 million grants' fits ~67% of 3m in 2025). It is a count share; dollar share not given.

claim_as_stated: NPact Standard Terms §2.4 (Aug 2025) bars access or 'donations, grants, transfers ... or payments' through third-party products; iPhi terms give data in 'industry-standard format for fifteen (15) days' after exit
exact_values_found: NPact 'Last updated: August 26, 2025' (changes of Aug 5 and Aug 26, 2025). '2.4 Rejection of External Passthrough. NPact does not authorize Customer or its subsidiaries, affiliates, employees, donors, grant applicants, ... vendors, board members or agents to access the Services or Software through third-party products or applications or initiate and/or authorize any actions including but not limited to communications, donations, grants, transfers, allocations or reallocations, or payments of any kind through third-party products or applications.' Ren MSA (party: Renaissance Acquisition Company LLC): on termination 'Ren will make available to Customer all Customer Content in an industry-standard format for fifteen (15) days, provided that after such period Ren shall have no obligation to continue to maintain Customer Content'.
discrepancies: Ellipsis drops 'allocations or reallocations'; immaterial. The Ren document is titled 'Final Draft' (2023-06-20 v2), a published template MSA, not confirmed as the executed terms for any customer; the PDF version at /2023/07/ now returns 404.
interpretation_challenge: NPact's clause is phrased as non-authorization ('does not authorize') rather than an enumerated prohibition with remedies; its practical force depends on breach/termination clauses. The 15-day window applies to 'Customer Content' (sponsor-entered data); negotiated order forms may override (MSA says Order Form/SOW prevails on conflict).

claim_as_stated: Daffy MCP server exposes make_donation with no documented per-donation limit; its CLI confirmation is skippable with --yes
exact_values_found: MCP: 9 tools 'scoped to your fund' incl. make_donation ('Moves real money') and cancel_donation ('Permanent'); no per-donation, daily or minimum limit stated; parameters not documented; API keys 'can move money in your fund', revocable at daffy.org/settings/developers. CLI: donate/gift create/cancel show a [y/N] prompt; '--yes' = 'Skip the confirmation prompt on donate, cancel and gift create'; docs say pass --yes 'only once the member has explicitly confirmed'; minimum donation $10, gift $18; no maximum stated.
discrepancies: None. Note the CLI does document a $10 minimum (a floor, not a limit).
interpretation_challenge: Absence of a documented limit is not proof of no server-side limit; donations are bounded by available fund balance, MCP clients that honour tool annotations prompt for approval, and cancel_donation works before payout. The real control gap is that limits are not documented, not that they demonstrably do not exist.

claim_as_stated: Flipcause: founder told court donations belonged to the company; Stripe froze a $1.45M reserve
exact_values_found: Oakland Voices: 'At Flipcause's Dec. 22 bankruptcy hearing, Flipcause Executive Chairman Emerson Ravyn testified that donations sent to charities through Flipcause belonged to the platform, not the nonprofits' (judge Thomas Horan's question answered 'Yes, that's cor[rect]'); CEO Sean Wheeler email: 'Flipcause owns the funds upon receipt'. Stripe objection opposed release of 'an estimated $790,000'; 'In bankruptcy filings, Flipcause lists the amount at $1.45 million'; Stripe says the reserve is 'less than $1 million' and cites up to ~$6m potential chargebacks/fines. MinistryWatch: Stripe 'froze a $1.45 million reserve account'.
discrepancies: $1.45M is the debtor's own scheduled figure; Stripe's filing puts the reserve below $1m (~$790k estimate). Stating 'Stripe froze a $1.45M reserve' as fact adopts the debtor's number. 'Founder' = Emerson Ravyn (formerly Valiao), co-founder and Executive Chairman at the hearing; testimony was at a bankruptcy hearing, not a trial.
contradictory_evidence: Stripe objection (secondary copy): https://oaklandvoices.us/wp-content/uploads/2026/01/stripe_objection_flipcause.pdf (could not be parsed directly; quoted via Oakland Voices).
interpretation_challenge: The testimony is the debtor's legal position on title (merchant-of-record theory), not a court finding. Primary docket documents were not retrieved; evidence is from local press quoting filings.

entity: Jasper Ridge Charitable Fund; TIAA Charitable; Donors Fund Inc
claim_as_stated: Jasper Ridge Charitable Fund ($1.43bn) ceased and transferred ~$1.32bn to Fidelity, Schwab, Dechomai and Vanguard; TIAA Charitable moved $138.5m (244 accounts) to RCF; Donors Fund Inc's FY2024 990 shows 6,290 DAFs and $315.8m despite DAFRC marking it closed
source_date: TY2022; short TY ending 2021-05-14; TY2024 (amended, filed 2026-03-12)
exact_values_found: JRCF TY2022: total assets BOY $1,428,861,718, EOY $4,335,338; DAF grants $1,318,968,752; Schedule N total FMV $1,319,068,001; liquidation/termination box X. Schedule I cash+noncash: Schwab $51.93m+$698.66m=$750.59m; Fidelity $4.07m+$544.78m=$548.85m; Dechomai $0+$23.70m; Vanguard Charitable $50,000 cash only; ~$0.2m to 9 operating charities. TIAA: TY2020 EOY 1,548 DAFs, $162.1m; Schedule N: $138,461,300 to Renaissance Charitable Foundation dated 2021-03-09 (liquidation method). Narrative: on 2021-05-17 a further $430,495 went to RCF, of which '$354,551 was transferred into 244 separate donor advised fund accounts' and $75,944 to the 'TIAA Charitable Director's Fund'; $86,511 wind-down reserve. Donors Fund Inc TY2024 AMENDED 990 (object 202600719349301710, AmendedReturnInd X): DAFs held 6,290; EOY DAF value $315,757,385; DAF contributions $648.4m; total assets $336.6m. Original TY2024 990 (202543219349328909) and TY2023 990 contain no Schedule D Part I. DAFRC dataset operating_status for EIN 474844275: 'Assume Sponsor Closed 2023'.
discrepancies: TIAA: the 244 accounts belong to the May-2021 residual transfer of $354,551, not to the $138.5m March-2021 transfer; at FY2020 TIAA had 1,548 DAFs, so '244 accounts' as the size of the migration is wrong. Repo line 'accounts were rebuilt one-for-one at the successor (244 accounts)' is therefore unsupported. JRCF: Vanguard received only $50k cash; Schwab ($750.6m) and Fidelity ($548.9m) took ~98%. Donors Fund: figures come from an amended return; DAFRC label is 'Assume Sponsor Closed 2023' (an assumption flag), plausibly caused by the original TY2023/TY2024 returns omitting Schedule D Part I.
contradictory_evidence: DAFRC also shows Donors Fund FY2022 DAF grants as 'Imputed' $97.6m whereas the TY2022 990 reports $266.7m.
interpretation_challenge: 'Ceased' for JRCF is a termination of the DAF program with a TY2023 990-PF thereafter; the entity may persist in another form. Donors Fund is a DAFRC processing artefact rather than a sponsor that 'reopened'.

claim_as_stated: Sponsor verified exit rate ~0.19%-1.48% per year by count; at-risk denominator 5,746 sponsor-years
exact_values_found: Independent recomputation: panel 8,751 rows / 1,594 EINs; rows by FY 2019:1,341, 2020:1,447, 2021:1,469, 2022:1,489 -> exposure 5,746 sponsor-years (rows in FY t-1 for exits FY2020-FY2023). Verification file: 100 candidates, all with exit FY2020-2023 (10/21/26/43). Tier A 11 -> 0.191%; A+B 69 -> 1.201%; A+B+C 85 -> 1.479%; all candidates 100 -> 1.740%. Matches sponsor-mortality-summary.csv. Removing 18 trailing-imputed post-exit rows from the denominator (5,728) gives 0.192%/1.205%/1.484%.
discrepancies: Repo labels the exposure as 'sponsor-years (FY2020-FY2023)'; the rows counted are FY2019-FY2022 (the at-risk years preceding FY2020-FY2023 exits).
contradictory_evidence: Exit dating lags actual cessation by ~1 year where DAFRC imputes a trailing row: JRCF ceased in TY2022 but is dated FY2023; TIAA dissolved 2021-05-14 but is dated FY2022.
interpretation_challenge: The 0.19% floor counts only organisational cessation; a sponsor that stops DAFs but survives (tier B) is the economically relevant 'exit' for donors, so 1.20% is the better central count rate. Candidate-generation depends on DAFRC panel gaps; exits hidden by DAFRC imputation (264 imputed rows FY2019-22) can be missed, so the upper bound is not a hard ceiling. Annual rates are pooled; FY2023 (2.2% upper) is higher than FY2020 (0.7%).

claim_as_stated: Fairbairn v. Fidelity Investments Charitable Gift Fund: donors lost at trial; Pinkert dismissed for lack of standing
exact_values_found: Fairbairn (N.D. Cal. No. 3:18-cv-04881-JSC): bench trial; Magistrate Judge Jacqueline Scott Corley ruled for Fidelity Charitable on 2021-02-26, finding plaintiffs failed to prove the alleged promises or negligence. Pinkert v. Schwab Charitable Fund, No. 21-16299, 48 F.4th 1051 (9th Cir. 2022-09-14): affirmed dismissal; donor lacked Article III standing to sue over fees/investment options.
discrepancies: None. 'Trial' was a bench trial before a magistrate judge (by consent), not a jury. Pinkert was against Schwab Charitable (repo should name the defendant).
interpretation_challenge: Fairbairn lost on the facts after surviving a standing challenge (2018 order rejected the AG-only standing argument), so it does not show donors lack standing; Pinkert does, in the Ninth Circuit, for fee/prudence claims. Together they show donor litigation is weak, not that it is barred.

entity: Fidelity Charitable; Vanguard Charitable; Schwab Charitable (DAFgiving360)
claim_as_stated: 2026 SPLC holds drew a letter from 16 attorneys general (California AG release 2026-05-22)
exact_values_found: CA release dated 2026-05-22: coalition of 16 AGs (CA, MN, CO, CT, DE, HI, IL, ME, MD, MA, NV, NY, OR, VT, VA, WA); names Fidelity Investments Charitable Gift Fund, Vanguard Charitable Endowment Program and Donor Advised Charitable Giving, Inc. as having 'either restricted or halted payments to the SPLC' after the DOJ indictment (2026-04-21). Minnesota AG Ellison led; MN release dated 2026-05-21.
discrepancies: Repo (industry-incentives-structural-analysis.md) says AGs wrote 'on May 22, 2026'; the letter/lead release is dated May 21, CA's release May 22.

claim_as_stated: Charityvest final audited FY2024 statements disclose a Foundation Source fee (~$653k) in a note
exact_values_found: Note 1: comprehensive services agreement with Vennfi, Inc., 'an affiliated for profit entity'; 'During 2024, Vennfi was acquired by Foundation Source Philanthropic Services Inc. ... and the agreement was maintained in place with Foundation Source. During 2024 and 2023, costs of $653,138 and $507,387 for services from Vennfi and Foundation Source were incurred with a balance due of $181,921 and $47,743'. Statement of functional expenses 2024: 'Platform fees' $653,137; total expenses $52,603,302; grants $51,791,362. Fee is 'monthly income ... at a certain agreed upon percent'; Vennfi/FS rebate shortfalls if needed.
discrepancies: The $653k is paid to Vennfi and Foundation Source combined for 2024 (Vennfi pre-acquisition plus FS after), not a pure Foundation Source fee. $1 rounding difference between note ($653,138) and expense statement ($653,137).
interpretation_challenge: Fee is ~1.24% of total expenses but is percentage-of-assets based; the agreement also has Vennfi/FS cover operating shortfalls, so the 'fee' is net of a subsidy arrangement and understates the vendor's economic role.

claim_as_stated: DAFRC 2026 adviser study (n=669): 35% recommend DAFs most of the time or always; TPI 2026: 51% of advised HNW clients use a DAF
exact_values_found: DAFRC: 'six focus groups and a national survey of 669 financial advisors'; 'Thirty-five percent of financial advisors in the study recommend DAFs most of the time or always, and 21% recommend DAFs about half of the time'; DAFs second most recommended after direct giving. TPI methodology: 300 advisors plus 'an online survey ... among 103 HNW clients who participate in philanthropic activities' ($5m+ investable assets), Dec 2025-Jan 2026; 'More than half (51%) use donor-advised funds'; 78% use at least one vehicle, '84% among HNW clients who discuss philanthropy with an advisor'.
discrepancies: TPI's 103 'clients' were screened on assets ($5m+) and philanthropic activity, not on having an adviser; the report separately gives 84% vehicle use for those who discuss philanthropy with an adviser. 'Advised HNW clients' (and the repo's 'advised and sponsor-linked sample') is therefore a mislabel; correct is '51% of 103 philanthropically active HNW individuals ($5m+)'. DAFRC study is published via DAFgiving360 (Schwab Charitable) and the repo cites secondary coverage.
interpretation_challenge: n=103 gives a ~±10pt margin; the report is hosted by The Boston Foundation and redistributed by Foundation Source (a DAF vendor). DAFRC 35% is an adviser self-report, not observed recommendation behaviour.
